name: Working with Chinese Manufacturers

claims.claim_text: Assembly houses stock the common passive values and will supply them from their own reels, which is cheaper than buying a full reel, but the substituted part carries whatever tempco and power rating the house happens to stock, so any passive with a real specification has to be called out.
claims.quote_verbatim: you've got to be careful that it's not a part which you need a specific, you know, spec for. So, they'll just use some generic, you know, part. And, yeah, you've just got to be careful. You know, it's got some different Temco or something like that. So, some different power rating to some other one
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: EE Movies, Part Rants and SPICE.

claims.claim_text: The common failure of first-time hardware companies is treating the factory as a black box that will turn a prototype into a product; factories employ real engineers but that is no guarantee they are better than yours, and handing a design over on faith is how projects go wrong.
claims.quote_verbatim: we're just going to go to China, and China will fix it. So we'll send them the prototype. China will fix it, and it will magically become a product. And so there's sort of this void of people that want to manufacture their own hardware just, you know, dumping stuff onto a factory and just assuming that it's going to be done right
claims.speaker: Joe Grand
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Joe Grand - Pancyclopaedic Prototyping Polymath

claims.claim_text: A factory may substitute capacitors or buy through a broker with counterfeit stock because of its own supplier relationships; the resulting failures appear months later with thousands of units in the field, and tracing them backwards is far harder than preventing them.
claims.quote_verbatim: a factory might swap in different capacitors because they have a relationship with the company. Yeah, the cheaper – Yeah, exactly. And then you run into the failure problem
claims.speaker: Joe Grand
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Joe Grand - Pancyclopaedic Prototyping Polymath

claims.claim_text: Face-to-face contact is what marks a customer as serious to a factory, and most people never go and introduce themselves, which is where much of the substitution risk originates.
claims.quote_verbatim: unless you have that face-to-face contact and the client knows – or the factory knows that, you know, you're a serious client
claims.speaker: Joe Grand
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Joe Grand - Pancyclopaedic Prototyping Polymath

claims.claim_text: The point at which startups engage a Chinese factory is typically the 80 percent point: a prototype that works for minutes, funding in place, and no idea how to pick a factory without losing money, IP, or a year.
claims.quote_verbatim: they're just starting to think about, geez, how do we pick a factory in China? How are we going to do this without getting screwed and losing everything from having somebody take our money, take our IP, and waste a lot of time
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Scott Miller - Sudden SinoAmerican Synthesis

claims.claim_text: Whether you can run Chinese production remotely depends on the product and your own track record; for a complex consumer product a beachhead in-country is close to a precondition, partly because the time difference leaves only two overlap windows a day.
claims.quote_verbatim: If you were building a swizzle stick for McDonald's and done it a thousand times, then you'd probably be fine, especially if you knew the factory. But as we found with the Roomba, there's – without having a beachhead in China, it would have been nearly impossible
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Scott Miller - Sudden SinoAmerican Synthesis

claims.claim_text: Flying in produces a burst of progress and then a stall: a visitor gets a tremendous amount done in a week, and when he leaves momentum stops, because physical presence at the factory is what closes the question-and-answer loop in real time.
claims.quote_verbatim: clients will fly over before they work with Dragon, and they'll get a tremendous amount done during that week. And then they'll fly home and another client from a different company will fly over and everything. And the first guy will stop and the second guy will take off. But it's just really hard to get any sort of momentum. So just being a physical presence right at the factory
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Scott Miller - Sudden SinoAmerican Synthesis

claims.claim_text: Under roughly a thousand units the labour saving is small relative to the overhead of managing China, and domestic manufacturing buys better IP protection and a faster design-build-test cycle.
claims.quote_verbatim: And if you're under 1,000 units, that would also make a lot of sense. You get typically much better IP protection in the U.S. And you can also go much faster
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Scott Miller - Sudden SinoAmerican Synthesis

claims.claim_text: Factories make their money on volume, so interest starts around 5,000 units and it is genuinely hard to get attention below that.
claims.quote_verbatim: Where you might think about China is if your units are 5,000 units and more. And part of the reason is the factories are a lot less interested for units under 5,000 because they make all their money on volume. The volume coming from the labor component and then also what's called their markup. So it's really hard to get their attention for that
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Scott Miller - Sudden SinoAmerican Synthesis

claims.claim_text: The decisive Chinese advantage over labour cost is supply-chain density: components and vendor capabilities for almost anything can be found inside the Pearl River Delta.
claims.quote_verbatim: In China, though, unlike the U.S., unfortunately, is just a remarkably robust and diverse supply chain. So you can find almost anything you want in terms of components, in terms of vendor capability, all within, let's say, the Pearl River Delta
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Scott Miller - Sudden SinoAmerican Synthesis

claims.claim_text: Hand processes that replace automation need process control to hold quality: soldering iron temperatures drift, so a written calibration procedure and worker training have to be imposed rather than assumed.
claims.quote_verbatim: in China, the temperature of the soldering irons drifts all over the place. So, you need a process procedure to go in and make sure that those are calibrated and the workers are trained
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Scott Miller - Sudden SinoAmerican Synthesis

claims.claim_text: Rather than spending NRE to automate an immature design, Chinese labour lets you hand-solder wire harnesses and through-hole parts; the price of that choice is that quality now depends on process discipline instead of machines.
claims.quote_verbatim: rather than spending all that NRE to take a design, which is probably not that mature to start with, and then add on automation on top of that, you're right. You can just go to China and solder the wire harness
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Scott Miller - Sudden SinoAmerican Synthesis

claims.claim_text: For a seasonal consumer product the schedule constraint is absolute: sales are exponential around Christmas, competitors' advertising has already set what children ask for, and every week of lateness removes the tall part of the curve.
claims.quote_verbatim: You absolutely cannot be late for the Christmas season because it's all exponential sales. And every week you're late, the tall part of the graph falls off
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Scott Miller - Sudden SinoAmerican Synthesis

claims.claim_text: One way to cost a product without access to Chinese pricing networks is to base the estimate on catalogue distributor pricing and local manufacture and then apply a multiple of about two and a half to three, treating any Chinese saving as upside rather than as the plan.
claims.quote_verbatim: The way I do it is that I base everything on DigiKey mouse-up pricing and I base everything on local manufacturing and then I add my typical, you know, times to half times three
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Scott Miller - Sudden SinoAmerican Synthesis

claims.claim_text: A turnkey arrangement concentrates the risk: hand a Chinese contractor the design, the money and the schedule, and if they do not produce there is nothing to fall back on.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can get screwed. I mean, you know, if you choose somebody in China, oh, yeah, we lay out. We do turnkey, you know. Yeah. And then you give them everything or your hopes and dreams and all your money, you know, that you mortgaged your house for and they don't produce
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Kickstarter, Manufacturing, Open Hardware - Judging Jurisdictional Junctures

claims.claim_text: Contract manufacturers generally farm out enclosure design and board layout to outside specialists, because their own competence is the assembly line rather than design.
claims.quote_verbatim: They farm out mostly everything. Because really their speciality is the manufacturing side of things. Right, right. They don't want to deal with the rest. It's the pick and place machine. Right. You know, they don't design 3D cases in-house usually. They'll give it to someone else. They don't lay out boards in-house
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Kickstarter, Manufacturing, Open Hardware - Judging Jurisdictional Junctures

claims.claim_text: Blaming a vanished contract manufacturer is a standard excuse from failed crowdfunded projects; the alternative is either hiring someone whose business is managing the factory or going over and supervising the build yourself.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you don't think to hire someone like Scott or if you don't go over to China and babysit the process
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Kickstarter, IndieGoGo & Ignite - Jasperated Jimswinger Jobbery

claims.claim_text: The reliable way to find a first manufacturer is a referral from someone who has already shipped with them, because it substitutes their filtering for your own trial and error.
claims.quote_verbatim: I just asked a friend of mine, like, hey, you've had some conference badges, electronic conference badges made. Who do you have manufactured those? You know, I got a referral. And I just tried these guys out. Eat a net. They're owned by somebody who lives in the Bay Area, but their operations are in Shanghai. And I had great experiences with them. Like, my first ever manufacturing went very smoothly or as smoothly as you could possibly imagine. Of course, there were minor hiccups. But I think I just kind of got – I kind of lucked out with a good referral early on
claims.speaker: Michael Ossmann
claims.episode_title: Interview with Michael Ossmann - Gifted Grimgribber Grokker

claims.claim_text: A couple of thousand units is small volume by Chinese standards, close to the point where factories will not engage, and the tooling rather than the assembly is what makes such a run expensive.
claims.quote_verbatim: a couple of thousand is small volume for China. I mean, almost to the point where they don't even want to talk to you
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Intense Illusion Introduction

claims.claim_text: There is a zone of pain between garage assembly and contract manufacture where the volume is too large to build by hand, too small to interest a factory, and the money raised is not enough to buy your way out of it.
claims.quote_verbatim: we managed to raise enough money that we avoided this sort of zone of pain that a lot of Kickstarter projects get into where you can't build them in the garage anymore, but you're not really interesting for a contract manufacturer. Uh, so you haven't got quite enough money to go elsewhere and you end up being screwed
claims.speaker: Andrew Witte
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Andrew Witte - Telistic Timepiece Technomania

claims.claim_text: Bringing a consumer product through a Chinese factory took ten to twelve trips, which stops being enjoyable after the first two or three; attempting the same project hands-off is described as impossible even for simple products.
claims.quote_verbatim: as part of the process, 10 or 12 tickets to China, way too many. It's fun the first two or three times and then it just becomes a drag. Yeah. But trying to do it without going over there and just totally hands off. No, that's impossible. I wouldn't want to do a, try and do a project that way. Even, even for simple things, it's, it's just not possible. It just blows up in your face every time
claims.speaker: Andrew Witte
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Andrew Witte - Telistic Timepiece Technomania

claims.claim_text: Custom machined and gold-plated parts that would require finding and qualifying vendors across a whole country in the United States sit within about half an hour of the final assembly factory in China, which is what compresses the iteration loop.
claims.quote_verbatim: we've got this charging connector on the side of the watch and it's got these pins that are custom machined and then we get them gold plated and like finding the machining shop and then the gold plating service and like we'd have to be flying all over the u.s to find vendors that could do this stuff whereas in china it's all within like half an hour drive of the factory
claims.speaker: Andrew Witte
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Andrew Witte - Telistic Timepiece Technomania

claims.claim_text: When a platform-defining part goes obsolete with no last-time buy, the sequence is to buy up world stock and then commission a manufacturer to copy the design and supply a compatible part, because changing the part would strand every module already built around it.
claims.quote_verbatim: we had to buy up the world stock. And once that was gone, well, you know, we're committed to this because it was the, you know, it was the plug-in platform that we were using. Right? That we had standardized on. So it's not like we just go choose another one because then all the modules we'd ever built weren't compatible anymore. Oh, jeez. Right? Yeah, right. So we had to go find a manufacturer who was willing to copy that existing design and manufacture us a compatible one
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A copied part is never an exact duplicate, so it has to be fully re-characterised: automated insertion jigs were built to mate the replacement connectors a thousand times at varying angles and measure gold wear and expected life.
claims.quote_verbatim: we had to fully re-characterize and re-test those connectors. And they were different. You know, we designed automated insertion testing jigs. So, it would make these connectors a thousand times at different angles. And we could see the result. You know, how much gold was it wearing off? How much, you know, how long would the thing last
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: A supplier who tools up for you while you are in a bind acquires pricing power: the tooling is already paid for and sitting in their plant, so re-tooling elsewhere costs more than the premium, and you pay the premium indefinitely.
claims.quote_verbatim: I could go pay tooling somewhere else and deal with headaches again. Or I could just keep paying this premium. And it's like, you're going to pay the premium every time
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: A reasonably sized contract manufacturer will let you design around the parts already loaded on their machines, which removes setup and sourcing cost from the build.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can actually design your product around the parts that they have available and sitting on the machine and all preloaded
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Last Minute Decisions - Obdurate Onepercenter Obstacles

claims.claim_text: Contract manufacturers, prototype houses and component vendors will not volunteer the full set of constraints up front, and asking a supplier what will go wrong with what they are selling does not produce an answer; the limits emerge from actually building.
claims.quote_verbatim: the only way to really get the answer is to actually build it and that you can't just ask somebody before you build it
claims.episode_title: MightyHohm For The Holidays - Kaiser Keyzer's Kits

claims.claim_text: A prototype house may quietly hand-solder a part to get your job out of the door and say nothing, so the process only fails when the order reaches a hundred thousand and the factory says it cannot be done; volunteering that kind of feedback is what separates a good contract manufacturer from a bad one.
claims.quote_verbatim: they sort of like hand soldered that part or they did this or they did that just to get the job done. And then it's not relevant to volume manufacturer until you hit like a, you know, a hundred thousand. You know, then when you give them an order for a hundred thousand, they go, oh, sorry, we can't really do that
claims.episode_title: MightyHohm For The Holidays - Kaiser Keyzer's Kits

claims.claim_text: US contract assembly runs about five to six cents per component placement, so a 500-part board carries several tens of dollars of placement cost alone and the annual figure runs into hundreds of thousands of dollars at modest volume.
claims.quote_verbatim: we're paying about five or six cents per placement, which I believe is pretty standard in the U S right. So I mean, it's every single part of your board. It costs five or six cents. Um, it's kind of medium, small volumes. Um, but when we, we, when we launched the new products, the, the number of parts on the board, cause they're analog and they're many, many channel analog, the, the number of parts, uh, like dramatically increased. And so, I mean, our logic eight product has like 500 parts on it
claims.speaker: Joe Garrison
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Joe and Mark Garrison - Subtly Spelling SayLeeAy

claims.claim_text: Choosing assembly equipment on a salesperson's account is a due-diligence failure; the checks that matter are running your actual board on the actual machine and picking a machine that working contract manufacturers use in daily production.
claims.quote_verbatim: build the actual board on the actual machine, um, select, select, select a machine that actual CEMs use every day in production
claims.speaker: Joe Garrison
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Joe and Mark Garrison - Subtly Spelling SayLeeAy

claims.claim_text: Outsourcing forces you to buy months of inventory in one lot to get a volume price, while in-house assembly allows building to order a few days ahead, which is a cash-flow argument rather than a unit-cost one.
claims.quote_verbatim: in order to get any sort of board volume, you have to go to a CM and say, well, we'll buy 500 or a thousand boards, which may last you a few months or something. Right. But if you have your own manufacturing, technically you could be a couple of days ahead and you could just be basically building to order
claims.speaker: Joe Garrison
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Joe and Mark Garrison - Subtly Spelling SayLeeAy

claims.claim_text: Conventional contract manufacturing works by throwing the files over the fence and letting the house set up and run the job; requiring the customer to approve every part before the machine starts moves that check to the one person who knows the design.
claims.quote_verbatim: Oh, so the client has to sign off on it before you press the go button. Absolutely. They have to approve all the parts on that. For those who aren't aware, that's not how regular contract manufacturing works. You sort of generally, like, throw it over the fence, give them all the files, and they're the ones who check it and set it up. Yeah, set up the pick-and-place machine and press go, and then you cross your fingers and hope the board comes out the other end with the parts in the right orientation
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An interview with Macrofab - Macro Manufacturing Mechanization

claims.claim_text: Sending a design to a contract manufacturer removes the option of walking onto the floor to clarify a detail, and every change after handover is billable, because change orders are where the manufacturer's margin is made.
claims.quote_verbatim: you need to be very confident when you send it out to a CM because anything else, that's how they're making their margins
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Inspirations and Aspirations - Recanting Rocket Rationale

claims.claim_text: The most effective tool for resolving problems at a Chinese factory is a camera good enough to photograph an actual defect, circle it, and email it to everyone at once, because a conference room rarely has a microscope and a photograph settles the argument.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's pretty much nothing more powerful than being able to take a photo of an actual defect or a problem and then email it to a bunch of people and say, okay, the problem is here and then circle it with a big arrow, right? Like that is probably the number one tool
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Everything needed for a factory trip should fit in carry-on, because checked luggage that arrives a day late costs a day of a trip that exists to compress the feedback loop.
claims.quote_verbatim: always bring what you can carry onto the plane because checked luggage can go missing
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Small personal consumables matter on a factory floor: locally supplied gloves and finger cots are sized for local hands, so bringing your own avoids improvising with equipment that does not fit.
claims.quote_verbatim: the kind that you get in China are typically too small for my fingers. And so I bring just my own
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Buying supplies locally during a factory trip can cost half a day to a market by taxi with a language barrier at the far end, so experienced visitors carry what they expect to need.
claims.quote_verbatim: then you've got to take a half day to get a taxi and get over there. And it takes a long time because you're, you know, you have trouble with the language and stuff like that
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: A larger contract manufacturer employs people whose job is supply-chain continuity, and the deliverable is a set of qualified alternates named in the design so no jelly-bean part is single sourced.
claims.quote_verbatim: so that you have supply chain continuity. So you don't have a single source component, especially for easy jelly bean stuff. They make sure that you've got a, a large number of alternates that you can specify in the design
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: At scale a manufacturer may need to build a line or open a factory to meet your demand, which takes so long that single-sourced components have to be fixed early rather than during a fast development cycle.
claims.quote_verbatim: a manufacturer may need to build an assembly line or open a factory that they didn't have before because they need to meet the demand. And that's something that requires a huge amount of time. And so, you know, if you're doing a really rapid development, it's hard to, to, to get all that kicked off while you're still doing component selection. So you sort of need to nail down a lot of things early in the process
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Stopping the line is the correct response when outgoing product would be compromised, and it is a finite resource: use it too often and the factory stops taking your calls.
claims.quote_verbatim: there are definitely cases where you stop the line, especially early in the process. Yeah. You don't you don't do it. I mean, eventually the factory is probably going to stop returning your calls
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Factories are used to dealing with remote design teams and their attendant delay, so a designer physically on site who can authorise a change becomes an unusually valuable resource to them and is treated accordingly.
claims.quote_verbatim: the factories are not used to the designer being there. Yes. So you sort of get a lot of respect and attention because they realize that you are this super high bandwidth source of information
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: A designer on the factory floor with the authority to decide can close changes in an afternoon that would otherwise take days or weeks, which is why sending a proxy produces a materially different result.
claims.quote_verbatim: I need to change this resistor. OK, it's done. And yeah, I have the authority to say that, yes, you need to now change that resistor. And so you can have things that happen in an afternoon that normally would have taken days or even weeks to do
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Component problems in China can usually be resolved within a day or two by getting the local manufacturer's representative to the factory, a level of vendor support that is not available at the same speed elsewhere.
claims.quote_verbatim: there seems to be no issue that within one or two days cannot be solved by bringing in like a local manufacturer's representative. Right. And, and having them provide support. And that's something that you're never going to get in the States at the same level
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: A factory with impressive equipment may quietly subcontract small orders to a cheaper shop and keep the margin, and the failure mode is that it does not quality-check the shop it subcontracted to.
claims.quote_verbatim: what they do. . . Is for small orders. They outsource it. They outsource it to. . . A small print. . . Like. . . They outsource it to a small print shop. And then. . . They keep the margin. But the thing is. . . They didn't do quality checks
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: A workable factory-selection procedure is to build a candidate list, request quotes, narrow the field on the quotes, and then visit; a factory that believes you are serious will readily host a tour.
claims.quote_verbatim: You can. . Like. . Come up with a list of factories. That you want to use. Or you want to like. . . Or you're interested in. You know. . . On Alibaba. And then. . . Get quotes from them. And like. . . . Kind of like. . . . Whittle down like. . . What you're interested in. And then. . . I think it's really important. That. . . Like. . . Once you talk. And you show interest. Then they'll be happy. To give you a tour
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Producing in China without a dedicated Chinese-speaking person on the ground goes badly even for people with prior manufacturing experience, and volume does not automatically imply China: capable partners exist in western Europe.
claims.quote_verbatim: china means that you have like if you don't have a dedicated uh chinese speaking person on the ground on the ground this is very important yep um you're not going to be able to pull things off if you don't have like prior manufacturing experience even if you have prior manufacturing experience but like arguably if you don't have a man on the ground things are going to be a mess

claims.claim_text: The realistic IP risk in Chinese manufacturing is not abstract theft but your design being produced alongside your own order, at another factory or on a night shift in the same one.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's a real risk of you know your ip being you know sure kind of leaked or whatever or you know literally taken to another factory and being produced side by side as well or in the same factory at night

claims.claim_text: For a first production batch it is almost always better to build somewhere you can walk to and look at, because a first batch of a new product will have problems that nobody has seen before.
claims.quote_verbatim: for the first batch, it's almost always better to, you know, do it somewhere where you can just walk down the street and see it
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Contract manufacturers earn their margin over the life of a programme, so quality can drift after the relationship settles; the counter is to keep visiting, confirm your line has not been moved to the basement, and resist the complacency that comes when builds are going smoothly.
claims.quote_verbatim: CMs make money on the margins, right? And over time, they usually make that margin on the backend
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: The counter to quality drift is periodic presence: visiting the factory to confirm your line has not been moved to the basement and that the job still has priority, precisely when everything appears to be running smoothly.
claims.quote_verbatim: how often should you visit the factory? Maybe things are fine, but it's important to kind of keep tabs. You want to make sure that your line hasn't been like relocated to the basement
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: At around 2,500 units a project can be stranded in a no-man's-land: too many to build by hand over weekends, too few to attract a contract manufacturer you would trust with the whole job.
claims.quote_verbatim: we're kind of in a no man's land with 2,500 units. We couldn't really find a CM that we were willing to hand everything over to

claims.claim_text: Contract manufacturers will give real design-for-manufacture feedback if asked, calling out things like vias buried under a QFN before the board is built, and mould designers will do the same for wall thickness and draft.
claims.quote_verbatim: Chris was, you know, willing to call out things like, you know, in your QFN you have these, you know, like buried vias or whatever. This is gonna have a bad time

claims.claim_text: Colour and finish are controlled with golden samples kept at the end of each production line, against which each batch is judged acceptable or not before it is fitted to shipping product.
claims.quote_verbatim: You have those golden samples that are sitting at the end of each manufacturer line to make sure that each batch that comes out is either acceptable or not before you start putting them on the backs of your product
claims.speaker: Alvaro And Jen From The Ure
claims.episode_title: An interview with Alvaro and Jen from the URE Podcast

claims.claim_text: Production ramp is staged deliberately: the first builds are run by the design engineers, then other people are trained on the product so they can answer problems on the line, because a handful of designers cannot stay in China indefinitely.
claims.quote_verbatim: the designers are just a handful. You can't have them in China 24-7 just making sure everything gets built. They do get sent, you know, to the factory to make sure it goes. But then you start training other people to, you know, understand the product and be able to respond to any problems that happen
claims.speaker: Alvaro Prieto
claims.episode_title: An interview with Alvaro and Jen from the URE Podcast

claims.claim_text: Contract manufacturers have specialities that are not advertised, so matching a factory to what you are actually trying to build is a real selection problem, and first-time builders rarely know how to navigate it.
claims.quote_verbatim: Different manufacturing houses have different capabilities. And, you know, obviously you have Flex and Foxconn as being the most visible ones worldwide. But they each have their own specialties. And it's not always obvious to most people when they're trying to find somebody, especially if it's the first time they're manufacturing something, that – how to navigate and find the right CM for what they're trying to do
claims.speaker: Alvaro And Jen From The Ure
claims.episode_title: An interview with Alvaro and Jen from the URE Podcast

claims.claim_text: Some smaller manufacturing houses invest free engineering iterations in startups they think are promising, effectively taking a position in the company's future volume rather than charging for the work.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's a number of smaller manufacturing houses that will kind of give you an internship, I don't know, like a prize. And they'll invest in what they think are promising startups. And they will give you kind of free work. They will work on your project for X number of iterations to kind of, you know, help and invest. But they're also kind of looking at it from their angle, like, hey, if this takes off, we can, you know, really make a lot of money here
claims.speaker: Alvaro And Jen From The Ure
claims.episode_title: An interview with Alvaro and Jen from the URE Podcast

claims.claim_text: Ramping quickly is possible in China because the components are made next door to the assembly, whereas nobody can overnight ten million parts from a catalogue distributor.
claims.quote_verbatim: In China, they make the components for the thing you're building right next to the thing you're building or, you know, nearby. So if you have to scale and you have to build, you know, a few million more this week, you couldn't do that in the U.S. You can't just go to DigiKey and overnight, you know, 10 million whatever components. But if you're near the factory of those, you could just drive down the road and get them
claims.speaker: Alvaro And Jen From The Ure
claims.episode_title: An interview with Alvaro and Jen from the URE Podcast

claims.claim_text: A precision injection mould for a small part is quoted at roughly $40,000 to $200,000 in a high-cost country, against Chinese injection-mould NRE quoted in the hundreds of dollars, which is the single largest cost difference in taking a plastic part to production.
claims.quote_verbatim: to have a mold for something like a small Lego brick made would probably be, I'm going to just take a guess, $40,000 to $200,000
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Advice to use the same tier-one contract manufacturer as a major consumer brand is usually bad advice for a small company, and it is often given by people who are expert at business but have never taken a physical product through production.
claims.quote_verbatim: in most cases, that's a very bad decision for a small company to use a large, you know, tier one CM
claims.speaker: Ben Einstein

claims.claim_text: Hiring people who have taken products through Chinese production before does not make a company successful, but it reliably reduces the number of avoidable mistakes, which is where most crowdfunded hardware projects actually die.
claims.quote_verbatim: they will guaranteed make fewer mistakes than doing it on your own. And so it's a very similar philosophy that we have, like having an engineer sitting with you doing, uh, you know, firmware review, um, or looking at, you know, board layout or, you know, helping you make sure you have as minimal, whatever slides and bizarre features on a plastic part, you know, it's not going to make you successful, but it's going to, it's less likely to make you fail
claims.speaker: Ben Einstein

claims.claim_text: A subcontracted cable assembly built with non-original connector housings had slightly smaller keying than the specified Molex part, which made it possible to plug the connector in reversed; that one orientation killed the first LED driver in the chain.
claims.quote_verbatim: they subbed out the manufacturer of these. Yeah, they got like a company to make up a plug with a tile and then got soldered onto the strips, which is, yeah, that's something you normally do. And what happened was that the connector housings they used, which weren't Molex, were much easier to plug into the connector the wrong way around. Because the keying was just a little bit smaller
claims.speaker: Mike Harrison

claims.claim_text: The failure needed several factors together: remote assembly, a substituted connector with weaker keying, and assembly workers with no reason to care whether it clicked in correctly; a single protection resistor on the affected input would have made the combination harmless.
claims.quote_verbatim: the fact it was being done remotely, the fact that the production connectors were very slightly different. And the fact that they were being assembled by people that may have not taken care to make sure it was plugged in the right way
claims.speaker: Mike Harrison

claims.claim_text: A hundred units is the practical inflection point for a foreigner engaging Chinese factories: the minimum order at which a factory will talk to you, still too small for them to want, accepted on the expectation you will grow, and the point where dinners with owners begin.
claims.quote_verbatim: A hundred is always the number that I think of for, particularly for foreigners coming to China doing manufacturing. It, that's sort of the inflection point where it starts to make sense to engage with factories and things like start doing dinners and start to meet owners
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: At low volume the cheaper path through a Chinese factory is often the white-label showroom: ask to modify something they already build rather than commission a design from scratch.
claims.quote_verbatim: at a hundred, it made a lot of sense to like, to, to ask for the white label room and be like, I want to modify this thing versus I want to make something from scratch
claims.speaker: Scotty Allen

claims.claim_text: A factory doing contract work is paid whether or not the product sells, which is why its incentives run to capacity utilisation and margin; the moment it makes its own white-label product it takes market risk it is not otherwise exposed to.
claims.quote_verbatim: if they're doing contract manufacturing work, like they get paid regardless of whether the product sells. Right. Right. Like that's not their responsibility. Whereas if they're making something like, uh, you know, Shanzai or like, or, or just, you know, white label or whatever that they're selling themselves, then they're taking a lot more risk
claims.speaker: Scotty Allen

claims.claim_text: One widely circulated rule of thumb is not to manufacture in China at all without roughly a hundred thousand dollars behind you, an argument made mainly on the cost of protecting intellectual property there.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's a great article on the China law blog. China law blog dot com about how basically don't go to China. Don't get stuff manufactured in China unless you have like a hundred thousand dollars
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Factories are classified by revenue: tier one at a billion dollars or more, tier two between $250 million and a billion, tier three below $250 million, where revenue means cost of goods times volume summed across product lines.
claims.quote_verbatim: when I think of tier one, I usually look at it in terms of a billion or more dollars in revenue and their revenue would basically just be the cost of goods sold of the product times, the volume of the product summed up across all their product lines. Uh, tier two would be 250 million to a billion. And then tier three is everything under 250 million
claims.speaker: Scott Miller

claims.claim_text: Tier-one factories can trace an individual serial number back to the reel a component came from and the lot and time window of the solder paste used; that traceability is what lets a return driven by a bad component be pinned down, and it is not available at tier three.
claims.quote_verbatim: they could track it all the way back to the particular reel that it came on the data was assembled and so on. And this gets so important from a quality standpoint that if you do have returns driven by a bad component, being able to pinpoint what happened, where is, uh, incredibly important. They also would track like the solder paste and they'd know this was from this lot. They kept it out, um, you know, to come up to temperature for four hours and they used it from three to five in the afternoon. Um, but yeah, just the level of tracking is insane, but you only really see that in tier one
claims.speaker: Scott Miller

claims.claim_text: Choosing a factory tier is a matching problem rather than a quality ranking: tier-three plants are lower-margin and more nimble without the overhead, and the right choice depends on your volume and what capability the product actually needs.
claims.quote_verbatim: trying to find the right match between what you're trying to do with your product and your volume, um, lined up with what a factory's, um, capability are. So you can get that, you know, that perfect, uh, impedance match
claims.speaker: Scott Miller

claims.claim_text: Contract assembly economics are dominated by setup charges of roughly twenty to thirty dollars per board once amortised over a small run, which can exceed the selling price of a simple low-volume board entirely.
claims.quote_verbatim: in contract manufacturing, it's all about the setup charges and whatnot. So, uh, the setup charges alone would be more per board than what we can even sell it for. So it could be 20 or 30 bucks just to set the machine up. If you amortize it across how many aren't you're making
claims.speaker: Ken Burns

claims.claim_text: Tariffs applied to raw components but not to finished goods invert the intended incentive: importing parts to assemble domestically attracts the duty while importing the completed product does not.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's actually cheaper if you manufacture it all in China and then you can sell, you know, ship the final iPhone and there's no tariffs associated with that. But if you import those raw materials and manufacture it in the U S it's actually 25% or whatever it is
claims.speaker: Ken Burns

claims.claim_text: A line-down event is the worst outcome in contract manufacturing because the idle line costs money without producing any, which is why companies will pull an engineer off holiday and fly them out to clear it.
claims.quote_verbatim: the worst thing that can happen when you're running a manufacturing line with a contract manufacturer is the line going down. And I'm not 100% sure of the fiduciary responsibilities that your company has to the contract manufacturer. That's a long way outside of my department. But basically, every day your line is sitting idle, it's costing you money and it's not making you any money
claims.speaker: Nash Reilly

claims.claim_text: Absent a specific and binding contractual prohibition, a Chinese manufacturer copying the product it builds for you is not in itself unlawful, and small customers rarely have the leverage or legal resources to impose such a contract.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's perfectly legal for your Chinese manufacturer to copy your products. End of story. Unless you have a really in-depth binding. Don't copy our shit clause in your contract
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: LEDs and EVs with Mike Harrison

claims.claim_text: Protecting a product in China is a matter of doing a few specific things differently, including registering a Chinese trademark, rather than relying on the NDA-style paperwork used elsewhere.
claims.quote_verbatim: register a Chinese trademark
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: LEDs and EVs with Mike Harrison

claims.claim_text: The publicised risk case is a highly funded crowdfunding project that goes to a Chinese manufacturer for cheap assembly and finds the product on sale before its own launch; how often this actually happens is less clear than the anecdotes suggest.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's been many articles over the years where these Kickstarters, you know, they've got in, you know, $10 million and everything. And they go to the Chinese manufacturer because they need to, like, assemble it cheap. And they all of a sudden find that it's on the market before they can even release it
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: LEDs and EVs with Mike Harrison

claims.claim_text: Custom cable assemblies are easy to obtain by finding an Alibaba supplier already making something similar and asking for specific changes; the difficulty is low volume, not customisation.
claims.quote_verbatim: go on Ali, Alibaba, find someone who's making something that looks relatively similar and write him an email and be like, Hey, can you change it here, here, and here
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Security steps delegated to the contract manufacturer as a final production step get missed: a shipping product from a major company was found with its debug interface unlocked because enabling the lock had been left to the factory.
claims.quote_verbatim: that was pushed to our contract manufacturer. Like that was the final production step
claims.speaker: Colin O'Flynn
claims.episode_title: Shouting at chips with Colin O'Flynn

claims.claim_text: On marketplaces such as Alibaba the selection heuristic that works is not lowest price but evidence the supplier will do a good job; the cheapest quote is the one to discard.
claims.quote_verbatim: You definitely do not want to go with the cheapest person. That's right. Typically, you want to find someone that you believe is actually going to do a good job
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: The Joulescope Upgrade with Matt Liberty

claims.claim_text: The fastest way through a supplier's drawing format for a custom part is to ask them to send a drawing in whatever form they already use and mark it up, rather than producing documentation in your own format.
claims.quote_verbatim: can you just send me a test or a drawing that you like? And I'll just mark it up
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: The Joulescope Upgrade with Matt Liberty

claims.claim_text: A one-person instrument business can split sourcing by process economics, buying CNC-machined aluminium enclosures from China because the domestic price is prohibitive while hand-assembling boards in batches of about fifty at home.
claims.quote_verbatim: the CNC aluminum enclosure for the, the box it sits in, I get that made in China. Uh, it's too costly in the UK to do that
claims.speaker: Ian Johnston

claims.claim_text: Contract assemblers ask customers to supply about ten percent excess on consigned parts, and about twenty percent on 0402 and smaller, to cover placement losses; expensive parts are excepted and covered only by enough for a few extra boards.
claims.quote_verbatim: How many excess parts do you tell customers you typically need? Okay. We're placing a thousand resistors. We need 1100 just because we're going to lose a hundred. What's, what's the 10%. We generally ask for 10%. Uh, for Oh, four or two is smaller. We ask for 20%
claims.speaker: David Ray
claims.episode_title: Electronics Manufacturing History with David Ray

claims.claim_text: An order for a hundred boards is built as 105 to 107, all of them tested, so the customer receives a hundred boards that passed rather than a hundred boards that were attempted.
claims.quote_verbatim: let's say you order a hundred. We'll make probably 105, 107. And, and, you know, give us QC procedure. We'll test all of them. And if all of them pass, you'll get all of them. Got it. You know, that way you're guaranteed to get the hundred working boards
claims.speaker: David Ray
claims.episode_title: Electronics Manufacturing History with David Ray

claims.claim_text: A design ordered from a Chinese supplier that was never documented on the customer's side can be lost entirely when the one person who knew the arrangement leaves; a major printer manufacturer reordered the same keypad for years with no design control over it.
claims.quote_verbatim: They never had design control. They never had it. Wow. Yep. It was just one guy. It was one guy
claims.speaker: David Ray
claims.episode_title: Electronics Manufacturing History with David Ray

claims.claim_text: Injection moulds are usually held by the manufacturer that cut them, so a plastic part cannot be moved to another supplier on price; changing supplier means paying for tooling a second time.
claims.quote_verbatim: usually the manufacturer holds the molds and things like that. Right. They're really expensive stuff. You can't just bugger off to another plastic supplier and say, give me 10,000 multimeter cases. Right. You've got to tool up again
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Chinese New Year shuts suppliers down for something like two weeks; orders placed just before it are accepted and then shipped whenever the plant restarts.
claims.quote_verbatim: A lot of companies are shutting down for, like, almost two weeks. And my PCB card is shut down. And I was ordering some parts from Alibaba last night. And they were shutting down. Oh, yeah, we'll happily take your order. But we'll, you know, ship it in two weeks' time. You get it when you get it
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Scheduling around Chinese New Year is routine practice: work involving Chinese suppliers is simply not started in late January, because the shutdown has been planned around for months at the other end.
claims.quote_verbatim: you just don't do something in, you know, late January, early to late January that involves China
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Component vendors want to hear a path to roughly 100,000 units before they engage, which is what makes vendor relationships hard for a company manufacturing at a few tens of thousands a year.
claims.quote_verbatim: They want to hear that you're going to be shipping around 100,000 units at some point
claims.speaker: Christina Cyr

claims.claim_text: One experienced practitioner's travel cadence is roughly three trips a year, batched so that he is physically present every time an injection-moulding tool is opened, which is the moment where a mistake is most expensive to discover late.
claims.quote_verbatim: he's doing trips over there. Yeah. Three times a year to get ready for holiday season. Exactly. Every time they're opening an injection molding tool, he's out there
claims.speaker: Scotty Allen

claims.claim_text: Chinese manufacturing has moved from taking Western designs to vertical integration, with camera modules, cables and enclosures for one product assembled in neighbouring buildings; the density means almost any part can be had immediately.
claims.quote_verbatim: you want a cable or a camera or, you know, a solar panel, or it doesn't matter what it is. You want a popcorn parts, you want a resistor, you want a capacitor. It's like, you can get it in a moment's notice
claims.speaker: Chrissy Meyer

claims.claim_text: Mechanical suppliers vary enormously in equipment, engineering skill and quality process, so a supplier that can technically make a part may still be unable to make it consistently; the electrical side is closer to binary, since a house either can place a given package or cannot.
claims.quote_verbatim: the suppliers, um, have dramatically, dramatically different equipment and different technical capabilities and dramatically different like quality processes in place. So even if they technically can make a part, um, they might not have like the skill on the engineering side, or they might not have the quality control in place to, to be able to do it consistently
claims.speaker: Chrissy Meyer

claims.claim_text: Shipping consumer hardware at scale meant months at a stretch camped on the assembly line, alongside picking the contract manufacturer, setting up the supply chain and the relationship dinners factory owners expect.
claims.quote_verbatim: being camped out on assembly lines in Shenzhen for like months and months at a time
claims.speaker: Chrissy Meyer

claims.claim_text: Even at a prototype quantity of four or five boards, paying a contract manufacturer around twelve hundred dollars to source and assemble them can be the right call, and it doubles as a rehearsal of the handover a volume house will require.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's like, yeah, let's just, let's just pay the, I think it's 1200 bucks
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Altium's relocation of its headquarters to China was made as a hard choice for existing staff, who were told to move or find another job; the company later found that low-cost high-quality software engineering there did not materialise.
claims.quote_verbatim: they made this massive move and people like you, Dave, were given the choice, you know, we want you in China or you can find another job
claims.episode_title: Publicly Traded Hobby with Ben Jordan

claims.claim_text: Moving a software organisation to China on the expectation of cheap high-quality engineers failed for Altium, a caution that applies to engineering headcount rather than to manufacturing.
claims.quote_verbatim: That's what Altium found out the hard way. They'd move their company to China thinking that they could get all these high quality, low, low cost software engineers. Failed miserably
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Wow, Dave REALLY likes Top Gun

claims.claim_text: A contract manufacturer that knows you from hundreds-of-thousands-unit programmes will not be interested in a few thousand units spread across five items, and the same relationship does not carry over to the smaller volume.
claims.quote_verbatim: we were doing hundreds of thousands of units. And I'm walking in with talking about thousands of units across five different items. They're a little bit less. They're just not going to care
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Intense Illusion Introduction
